title: Wastewater sequencing enables scalable measles surveillance
desc: Integrated clinical and wastewater monitoring during the 2024–2025 outbreaks of measles in South Africa enabled high-resolution tracking of virus spread and evolution. Whole-genome amplicon sequencing of wastewater samples revealed shifts in genotype prevalence, detailed transmission links and previously unreported interprovincial spread.

title: Risk governance for generative AI mental health support: a multi-turn safety architecture
desc: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for mental health support despite lacking mechanisms to safely govern evolving risk. Existing safety approaches primarily detect risk but rarely shape how models respond as conversational risk unfolds. We developed a portable, model-external safety governance architecture that combines contextual risk detection, reasoning-based verification, and protocol-guided response generation for multi-turn mental health interactions. Using synthetic conversations grounded in real-world mental health narratives, the architecture’s performance was assessed with GPT-5-chat and Qwen3.5-27B, increasing clinician-preferred escalation responses by 25.6–59.2 pp, while achieving high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85 (95%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity: 0.92 (95%CI: 0.89;0.95)). Performance remained stable across conversation length and across models (proprietary and open-source), with preliminary evidence showing that rapport and connection were preserved. These findings demonstrate that clinically-grounded governance can extend beyond risk detection to improve how LLMs manage evolving mental health risk, providing a framework for scalable safety governance.

title: Generating proteins with computationally predicted functions and multiple states via multimodal diffusion
desc: Generating proteins with the full diversity and complexity of functions found in nature is a grand challenge in protein design. Here we present protein diffusion transformer (ProDiT), a multimodal diffusion model that unifies sequence and structure modelling paradigms to enable the generation of proteins with computationally predicted functions at scale. Trained on sequences, three-dimensional structures and annotations for 128 million proteins across the evolutionary landscape, ProDiT generates diverse, novel proteins that are computationally predicted to preserve known active- and binding-site motifs and can be conditioned on a wide range of molecular functions, spanning 463 Gene Ontology terms. We introduce a diffusion sampling protocol to design proteins with multiple functional states, and illustrate this protocol by computationally scaffolding enzymatic active sites from carbonic anhydrase and lysozyme such that they are predicted to be deactivated by a calcium effector. Our results showcase the capacity of ProDiT to satisfy design specifications inaccessible to existing generative models, thereby expanding the protein design toolkit.

title: Zero-code deep learning platform for diagnosing tuberculosis and COVID-19 via chest X-ray findings.
source: PubMed · The Libyan journal of medicine
desc: [The Libyan journal of medicine] Thoracic infections are deemed extraordinary cases that need to be detected early to improve their corresponding management. Among these, tuberculosis (TB) and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) are the most dangerous and highly transmissible infections. They overlapped during the COVID-19 outbreak. One of the major diagnostic tools is the chest X-ray (CXR), which is attainable in most of the healthcare centers worldwide. Artificial intelligence (AI) has facilitated and improved the prediction of these and other diseases in recent years. Hence, the present study aimed to deploy a deep learning approach to predict TB and COVID-19 in comparison with healthy controls via CXR images. Google's Inception v3 model was used as the embedder, reputable for its speed and accuracy in image classification. Orange data mining software was utilized for the implementation of a deep neural network for diagnostic purposes of 268 each for controls, TB, and COVID-19 cases, while extracting 100 cases from each class for further external validation. A total of 100 neurons for 200 iterations and adaptive momentum (Adam) were used as the solver. The area under the curve (AUC) scored 1, while the accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-statistic were 98%. Upon internal validation for 300 cases, the constructed model displayed a slight drop in performance, with the AUC and other metrics decreasing to 0.997 and 0.967, respectively. However, the AUC and accuracy dropped to 0.88 and 66% after external validation. These findings highlight its potential as a diagnostic support tool while emphasizing the need for broader external validation and improved generalizability before clinical implementation.

title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
desc: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

title: MedDx, a training-free AI phenotyping model, identifies alcohol use disorder in cirrhosis with hepatologist-level agreement
desc: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is often under-documented in patients with cirrhosis, which delays treatment. Expert chart review of clinical notes can identify under-documented AUD, but is not scalable. We propose MedDx, an open-weight, training-free, and engine-agnostic language model, to phenotype AUD using clinical notes in patients with cirrhosis. We benchmarked MedDx on a 485-patient study cohort sampled from the 14,406-patient Indiana Cirrhosis Registry, using a chart-review-based reference as ground truth. MedDx agreed with the ground truth at three-class Cohen's {kappa} 0.92, against 0.67 for the AUD diagnosis code. It agreed with one hepatologist at 0.85 on all 485 charts and with a second at 0.82 on 186 charts, on which the two hepatologists agreed at 0.87. Weighted to the registry, its sensitivity was 98% and specificity 94%, against 63% and 96% for the AUD diagnosis code, and 61% of an estimated 6,223 patients with AUD had no AUD diagnosis by the first cirrhosis diagnosis. MedDx is openly available as an off-the-shelf, equitable, and auditable tool to identify AUD.

title: GinsengMind: An evidence-grounded AI research agent for integrative molecular research in Panax ginseng
desc: Panax ginseng C. A. Meyer is one of the most extensively studied medicinal plants, with substantial pharmaceutical and economic importance owing to its diverse bioactive constituents, particularly ginsenosides. Despite considerable advances in ginseng molecular research, the fragmentation of genomic, transcriptomic, protein structural, and biochemical information remains a major challenge for investigating gene function and specialized metabolism. Here, we developed GinsengMind (https://ginsengai.nrc.ac.cn), an evidence-grounded AI research agent that integrates species-specific molecular knowledge with large language model (LLM)-guided tool orchestration and structured retrieval-augmented generation. Built upon the telomere-to-telomere reference genome of P. ginseng, GinsengMind integrates 77,266 genes, 154,754 transcripts, and 77,266 protein records. Comprehensive functional annotation using Swiss-Prot, eggNOG, and InterProScan covered 97.00% of the 76,947 quality-controlled proteins. The platform further incorporates 71,046 ESMFold-predicted protein structures, 7,263,004 gene expression records across 94 RNA-seq samples, and 4,813 bibliographic records. Six specialized research tools enable autonomous evidence retrieval and source-linked scientific interpretation through natural-language interaction. To evaluate its performance, we established GinsengBench, comprising 50 curated questions across six research categories. In a blinded evaluation by three experts, GinsengMind achieved a mean weighted composite score of 96.18 across ten core questions, substantially exceeding GLM-5.3 without database access (23.24; mean paired difference, 72.94; 95% confidence interval, 65.19-79.87). Across five shared questions, GinsengMind outperformed nine general-purpose LLMs on average and achieved a score (96.56) close to that of GLM-5.3 supplied with predefined evidence packages (96.88), highlighting the importance of domain-specific knowledge and autonomous evidence retrieval. A case study of the ginsenoside biosynthetic enzyme PgUGT94Q2 further illustrates how integrated molecular evidence can reveal unresolved biological relationships and identify priorities for subsequent experimental investigation. Beyond conventional database querying, GinsengMind provides a foundation for exploring potential biological associations, prioritizing candidate biosynthetic genes, and formulating experimentally testable hypotheses. title: Sports agnostic whole body sweat rate prediction using consumer-grade wearables and biophysics-guided machine learning
desc: This manuscript describes a novel consumer-grade wearable approach, leveraging a self-supervised learning architecture for sports agnostic (basketball, running, soccer, and tennis) activity intensity features, that integrates with a heat balance approach to predict whole-body sweating rate. We collected whole-body sweating rates and analyzed data from 234 trials from 147 volunteers. Wet-bulb globe temperature ranged from 11 to 35 oC. Wearable triaxial accelerometry and chest-strap heart rate data were processed through a pretrained neural network to predict metabolic components for heat balance equations. For the independent validation set, the mean absolute error for predicted whole-body sweating rate was 0.08 L/h for basketball, 0.17 L/h for soccer, 0.00 L/h for tennis, 0.03 L/h for running with 0.03 L/h for all sports combined. The accounted-for variance (R2) for the whole-body sweating rate predictions were 0.76 for basketball, 0.73 for soccer, 0.82 for tennis, 0.94 for running and 0.79 for all sports combined. This study produced the following novel advancements: (1) first integration of wearable-derived activity features with a heat balance equation for sweat prediction; (2) first validated sport-agnostic wearable sweat prediction approach; and (3) first wearable method enabling a priori hydration management planning for exercise-heat stress conditions.

title: Exploring nonlinear body oscillations for natural quadruped gaits
desc: Animals’ body morphology shapes the gait patterns they can perform, where mechanical resonance reduces the need for active control. By tuning posture and muscle stiffness, they leverage their embodied intelligence to achieve effective gaits for different speeds. By contrast, most quadruped robots are not specifically designed to exploit mechanical resonance owing to the complexity of nonlinear dynamics and require dedicated locomotion controllers. To provide an alternative, we present a proof-of-concept framework making the nonlinear dynamics of a robot predictable in the design process and show how this knowledge can be leveraged such that multi-gait locomotion can emerge from nonlinear resonances—shaped by gravity, inertia and elasticity. Here we present the highly compliant quadruped robot eBert, on which we identify six nonlinear normal modes using our new theoretical tools and validate their existence in simulation and hardware. With black-box optimization to determine step length, simulations show how each nonlinear normal mode naturally develops into a distinct gait, manifesting different speeds, which also largely transfers to the robotic hardware. Our experiments show that eBert can exploit its mechanics to generate task-specific movements, which may serve as foundation for designing a new generation of agile and efficient robots leveraging embodied intelligence.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision diagnosis and management of cutaneous lupus erythematosus: from lesion recognition and multi-omics profiling to clinical decision support.
desc: [Frontiers in medicine] Cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) poses challenges in differential diagnosis, subtype classification, and longitudinal management because of its heterogeneous phenotypes and variable association with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). This narrative review evaluates artificial intelligence (AI) evidence by clinical task, data modality, disease relevance, and validation maturity. Direct CLE studies provide early evidence for image-based lesion and subtype classification, including a multicentre multimodal system that improved dermatologists' diagnostic accuracy. A separate proof-of-concept study used natural language processing (NLP) to estimate Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus Disease Area and Severity Index (CLASI) activity and damage scores from physical-examination notes. This text-based result should not be interpreted as automated severity scoring from clinical photographs: image-based lesion segmentation and CLASI estimation remain proposed applications. CLE transcriptomic, single-cell, and spatial studies reveal subtype-related B-cell signatures, interferon-associated keratinocyte states, specialized fibroblasts, and altered cell-cell communication; these findings are biological foundations for future models rather than validated patient-level prediction systems. Across applications, the level of CLE relevance is distinct from the maturity of validation. Current limitations include small or incompletely characterized disease-specific subsets, inconsistent image acquisition, uncertain independence of test cohorts, and limited prospective assessment of clinical utility. Progress requires transparent reporting of CLE-specific denominators, patient-level data separation, independent external validation, calibration, pigmentation-aware subgroup assessment, and clinician-supervised prospective evaluation. AI should therefore be regarded as an investigational decision-support approach for CLE, with clinical benefit established through disease-specific testing.

title: DiabetIA: A Longitudinal Electronic Health Record Dataset for Diabetes Research from Mexico
desc: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) from primary care are scarce in low- and middle-income countries, and few have been made available to researchers in Latin America. We present DiabetIA, a longitudinal dataset derived from the primary care records of the Mexican Institute of Social Security (IMSS). The first release comprises 136,674 adults followed in six IMSS family medicine units in the state of Michoacan between 2005 and 2020, with more than 3.2 million visits summarized in 414,770 two-year windows with at least one visit. Each window includes demographics, ICD-10 diagnoses, anthropometry, vital signs, laboratory results and prescriptions, and type 2 diabetes diagnoses in the following year as prediction targets. At baseline, 24.4% of the patients had type 2 diabetes, 37.1% hypertension and 32.3% obesity. Technical validation assessed completeness, plausibility, consistency, temporal coverage and agreement with a state health survey. DiabetIA is freely available for download to support research on chronic disease trajectories and prediction in an underrepresented population.

title: Automated benchmarking with structured variant effect data
desc: Protein variant effect prediction (VEP) has a wide range of applications, from describing the role of mutations in human disease to improving enzymes for industrial applications. VEP is now predominantly powered by machine learning models and high-throughput experimentation. Progress in this field depends on fair and systematic model comparison, which is complicated by the heterogeneity of VEP tasks and the diversity of model implementations. ProteinGym is the most widely used VEP benchmark, but it does not have a standard representation for datasets or models. This makes it difficult for others to run their own benchmarks with it and for the benchmark to keep up with new datasets and models. We address these shortcomings with the ProteinGym framework (PGF), which standardizes dataset representations, model interfaces, and evaluation protocols. The PGF consists of two packages: proteingym-base, which provides schemas for composing datasets and the PGDATA archive format, a standardized representation of VEP datasets, and proteingym-benchmark, which provides automated benchmarking of containerized models. As an example of a new experiment, we use the PGF to measure the ability of three supervised models to identify variants with property values that exceed those in the training set, a common objective in protein engineering. The PGF is available at https://github.com/ProteinGym.

Safety and accuracy diverge across deployment conditions in clinical large language models
desc: Clinical large language models (LLMs) are commonly scaled by increasing model size, context length, retrieval complexity, or inference-time compute, on the assumption that higher accuracy implies safer behavior. In medicine, where a few confident or evidence-contradicting errors can outweigh average performance, this assumption may be incomplete. We introduce Safety-Focused Evaluation of Scaling (SaFE-Scale) and instantiate it on RadSaFE-200, a 200-question text-based radiology multiple-choice benchmark with clinician-defined clean evidence, conflict evidence, and option-level labels for high-risk error, unsafe answer, and evidence contradiction. Thirty-four local LLMs were evaluated across six deployment conditions spanning closed-book, evidence-grounded, standard and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and max-context prompting. Clean clinician-written evidence, used as an upper-bound, produced the strongest joint gain, raising mean accuracy from 73.5% to 94.1% and reducing high-risk error from 12.0% to 2.6% and dangerous overconfidence from 8.0% to 1.6%. Standard and agentic RAG, max-context prompting, and inference-time compute improved selected metrics but did not reproduce this safety profile. Clinically consequential errors concentrated in a small subset of questions, and variance decomposition placed deployment condition above model family on every safety metric. Within this evaluation, clinical LLM safety did not track accuracy scaling but emerged as a deployment-level property.

title: Research hotspots and trends in machine learning for predicting postoperative outcomes of genitourinary cancers: A visualization analysis based on knowledge graphs.
source: PubMed · Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine
desc: [Technology and health care : official journal of the European Society for Engineering and Medicine] Background Machine learning has been increasingly applied to predicting postoperative outcomes in genitourinary cancers. However, a comprehensive understanding of the research landscape, major hotspots, and emerging trends in this field remains limited.ObjectiveTo analyse the research status, hotspots and future trends of machine learning in predicting postoperative outcomes of genitourinary cancers.MethodsEnglish-language studies published up to 30 May 2026 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. Annual publication trends were analysed using Excel, and VOSviewer and CiteSpace were used to visualise authors, countries, institutions, co-cited references and keywords.ResultsA total of 296 publications were included. Annual publication output showed an overall upward trend from 2021 to 2025, with a marked increase in 2025. China and the United States were the leading contributors, followed by England and Italy. The University of Texas System, Sun Yat-sen University, and the University of California System were among the most productive institutions. Co-citation analysis identified an interdisciplinary knowledge base encompassing cancer epidemiology, clinical guidelines, prognostic risk assessment, radiomics, and artificial intelligence. Keyword analyses highlighted machine learning, prostate cancer, deep learning, prognosis, and survival prediction as prominent research themes, with increasing attention to model evaluation, survival outcomes, and treatment planning.ConclusionThe bibliometric findings suggest increasing research attention to multimodal data integration, external validation, and clinical translation. However, further prospective studies are needed to establish whether these developments translate into meaningful improvements in clinical decision-making and patient outcomes.

title: LifeLine.ai: A SigLIP-MedGemma Multimodal Framework with KTO Alignment for Open-Vocabulary 12-Lead ECG Report Generation
desc: Automated twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has historically relied on discriminative classifiers limited to closed-set diagnostic labels, signal reconstruction, or saliency heatmaps. While categorizing predefined arrhythmias well, these static classifiers cannot generate narrative clinical reports, incorporate patient history, or support interactive clinical question-answering (Q&A). We present LifeLine.ai, an end-toend multimodal Vision-ECG-Language framework for automated cardiac diagnosis and clinical reporting. After early attempts at waveform peak-tracking and coordinate mapping failed against complex morphological variations, we leveraged large-scale PhysioNet repositories (MIMIC-IV and PTB-XL). Because hardware limits precluded training on over 800,000 raw records, we curated a balanced subset to estimate performance, converting one-dimensional signals into 3x4 twelve-lead grids with continuous Lead II rhythm strips at the bottom. Our pipeline integrates YOLOv11s localization, a LoRAadapted Google SigLIP encoder, a trainable Multi-Layer Perceptron projector, and a 4-bit quantized MedGemma-4B model, complemented by a separate Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) pipeline built on collected user feedback and a multi-LLM consensus engine. On this compact subset, SigLIP outperformed Swin Transformer encodings (~0.21 vs. ~0.25 validation loss), achieving 71.0% open-vocabulary precision and a 75.0% contextual F1 score across a cloud deployment spanning Vercel, mobile apps, Amazon EC2, Firebase, Hugging Face, Modal GPUs, and lifelinecg-sdk. Our code is available at https://github.com/Asad939asad/ LifeLine.ai-.

title: GRACE: Discrete Biological Sequence Optimization with Gradient-Resolved Adaptive Constrained Exploration
desc: Machine learning increasingly enables biological sequence redesign for therapeutic and biotechnological applications by optimizing sequences for desired properties. However, improving one property can compromise another: for example, increasing enzyme activity may reduce stability, while enhancing regulatory DNA activity may diminish cell-type specificity. We formulate sequence redesign as a constrained optimization problem guided by learned predictive models, where a reference sequence is mutated to improve a predicted target property while keeping predicted auxiliary properties within specified tolerances of their reference values. To solve this problem, we introduce GRACE (Gradient-Resolved Adaptive Constrained Exploration), a method that optimizes discrete biological sequences using gradients from property predictors via a straight-through estimator. GRACE combines two complementary mechanisms: null-space projection, which removes target-gradient components that interfere with active constraints, and an augmented Lagrangian mechanism, which encourages feasibility after constraint violations. We evaluate GRACE across fourteen diverse tasks, including six protein optimization tasks (spanning activity, stability, and solubility), five DNA tasks (spanning cell-type-specific enhancer activity, heat-shock-responsive promoters, and tissue-selective splicing), and three RNA design tasks (spanning translation efficiency, RNA folding, and toehold-switch function). Across these tasks, GRACE consistently achieves larger improvements in predicted target properties than discrete and continuous baselines while satisfying predicted auxiliary constraints. Together, these results establish GRACE as a general framework for machine-learning-guided biological sequence redesign under competing property constraints.

A long-context generative foundation model for versatile RNA design
desc: Programmable design of RNA sequences with defined functions remains a central challenge in biology. Despite recent advances, existing RNA generative models lack robust controllable design capabilities and are constrained by short context windows, limiting their capacity to model the complex evolutionary manifold of full-length transcripts. Here we introduce EVA (Evolutionary Versatile Architect), a long-context generative RNA foundation model trained on over 114 million full-length RNA sequences spanning the full breadth of evolutionary diversity. By integrating a mixture-of-experts architecture with an 8,192-token context window, EVA learns a unified, evolution-consistent representation of the RNA sequence space that captures both global transcript structure and fine-grained functional elements. EVA establishes a unified framework for a broad spectrum of RNA design tasks within a single architecture, ranging from mutational fitness prediction to context-aware sequence engineering. We demonstrate EVA’s versatility through de novo design and targeted optimization of diverse RNA classes, including transfers RNAs, aptamers and CRISPR guide RNAs, as well as messenger RNA and circular RNA therapeutics. In wet-lab assays, our best designed aptamers improve both fluorescence intensity and binding affinity by roughly twofold over the positive control. In systematic evaluations, EVA achieves state-of-the-art performance across seven of nine established benchmarks, generating sequences with more than tenfold lower Kullback–Leibler divergence to natural RNA secondary-structure feature distributions than the previous open-source RNA generator.

title: MRI-Based Radiomics and Deep Learning for Myometrial Invasion Prediction in Endometrial Carcinoma: A Narrative Review.
source: PubMed · Cancer control : journal of the Moffitt Cancer Center
desc: [Cancer control : journal of the Moffitt Cancer Center] Endometrial carcinoma is a common gynecological malignancy in developed countries, with its incidence continuing to rise. Myometrial invasion depth is a key prognostic factor and determinant of the 2023 International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging system, directly influencing surgical planning and adjuvant therapy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers excellent soft tissue resolution, but conventional interpretation remains limited by subjectivity and inter-observer variability. Radiomics and deep learning have emerged as promising tools for preoperative assessment. In this narrative review, we synthesize evidence from MRI-based studies, covering T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), contrast-enhanced (CE) MRI, multi-sequence approaches, and comparisons with radiologist performance. Key challenges include overfitting, lack of external validation, reliance on manual annotation, and limited interpretability. Reported performance varied widely. A recent meta-analysis suggested that pooled areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) are lower than those reported in the best-performing single-center studies, raising generalizability concerns. This review critically appraises current evidence, compares artificial intelligence (AI) with radiologist performance, and outlines a roadmap toward clinical translation, including multi-center harmonization, automated workflows, and interpretability-by-design.

title: Reproducible variability: assessing human vs. AI discordance in attempting to reproduce the same observational study
desc: Objective: Previously, nine expert teams given a published study and identical code sets produced nine substantially different cohorts, prompting the conclusion that analytic code cannot be reliably generated from natural-language description. We tested whether an artificial intelligence (AI) agent, given that same description, reproduces a cohort definition more faithfully and consistently than those teams. Materials and Methods: Against a claims database of 35.9 million patients, we executed 27 independent reproductions of that published glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist cohort definition: the nine published human definitions re-implemented deterministically (Arm A); nine independent AI agent runs given the source paper as published (Arm B); and nine given a rewrite that removed its internal contradictions (Arm C). All arms received identical frozen code sets. Agreement with a reference cohort was quantified by the Jaccard index. Results: Agents in Arm B achieved a median Jaccard index of 0.450 versus 0.259 for the human definitions, median pairwise agreement of 0.492 versus 0.149, and a 5.06-fold versus 32.0-fold size spread. Agent variation resolved almost entirely onto two criteria reported differently in the source main text and supplement. In Arm C, median agreement and median pairwise agreement both reached 1.000. Discussion: Changing only the analyst strongly trended towards improvement in fidelity, with every agent run more self-consistent than every human team. Changing the specification resulted in exact fidelity and self-consistency. Irreproducibility arose from both specification quality and inter-analyst variation. Conclusion: AI agents were more consistent than human teams when translating published natural-language descriptions into code.

title: GeneArbiter improves plant genome annotations while preserving established gene models
desc: As plant genome resources expand, updating established annotations requires incorporating improved gene models without disrupting correct structures or stable identifiers. We developed GeneArbiter, an evidence guided framework that treats annotation updating as a correction preservation problem. GeneArbiter uses the current annotation as a backbone, integrates alternative models with RNA splice junction and homologous protein evidence, and applies constrained language model arbitration followed by deterministic release and identifier reconciliation. In rice MH63, GeneArbiter recovered 4,701 reference loci missed by the current annotation while losing 1,890 current exact loci, yielding a net gain of 2,811 exact matches and increasing the gene level exact hit rate from 70.77% to 77.77%. It retained 97.54% of protein coding genes in the mature TAIR12 annotation and improved protein set quality metrics across 16 plant genomes. Independent transcript and protein evidence further supported GeneArbiter selected structural revisions at reference discordant loci. These results establish GeneArbiter as a conservative and traceable framework for maintaining plant genome annotations as new predictions and biological evidence accumulate.

title: 2项医生助手标准来了！《医疗健康行业智能体通用技术要求》上新_医疗人工智能
Artificial intelligence as a precision diagnostic tool in gastrointestinal pathology.
desc: [Histopathology] Personalized medicine is on the rise, leading to increasingly granular treatment options. Consequently, pathologists are required to provide more detailed diagnoses to fully use the potential of these novel therapies. The number and complexity of grading systems and biomarker scoring methods are increasing. At the same time, the resulting rise in workload coincides with a growing shortage of pathologists, highlighting the need for new methods to ensure high-quality patient care in the future. This review explores the feasibility and readiness of artificial intelligence (AI) applications to alleviate routine diagnostic tasks in gastrointestinal (GI) pathology. It provides an organ-by-organ overview of both non-neoplastic and neoplastic diseases, with an emphasis on tools that show promise for direct or near-term clinical implementation. We found that numerous studies have investigated a wide range of diagnostic challenges, many of which have yielded encouraging results. While most tools remain in the research phase and often lack multicentre validation, commercially available AI solutions already exist for certain applications, in some cases even with regulatory approval for routine diagnostic use. In conclusion, most AI applications in GI pathology are still at a relatively early stage, and several challenges remain to be addressed. Nevertheless, many studies report promising results and suggest substantial advances in the near future. These developments have the potential to benefit both pathologists and patients by significantly expanding diagnostic capabilities while improving accuracy and reproducibility.

title: How many large language models does title-abstract screening need? Theory, two replications and an evaluation at real prevalence
desc: Background and Objectives: Researchers increasingly combine large language models (LLMs) to screen titles and abstracts, assuming that more models make screening safer. We estimated how many models a screening ensemble needs, given correlated errors, and tested the answer on independent reviews and at real prevalence. Methods: We modelled correlated votes with a beta-binomial model and estimated, by bootstrap, the smallest ensemble capturing 95% of the net-benefit gain attainable over the best single model, accounting for human reading time and machine cost. Eleven LLMs from four developers voted blind on records from 13 SYNERGY reviews (derivation). We tested predictions fixed in advance on 10 and 16 Cochrane reviews from a public screening benchmark (replications) and evaluated a two-voter pipeline with an adjudicator on 11 complete benchmark collections and six reviews published in 2026. Results: Errors on relevant records were correlated (intraclass correlation 0.56 among eight different models; 0.75-0.78 among roles or copies of one model): eight models carried the information of about 1.6 independent ones. In derivation, the best single model, pair and trio reached sensitivities of 0.920, 0.975 and 0.981. Three or fewer models captured 95% of the attainable gain in at least 86%, 88% and 80.8% of bootstrap replicates of every scenario in the derivation set and the two replications, respectively. Six of seven registered predictions held in replication 1 and three of five sealed predictions in replication 2, where a fourth model added 2.1 percentage points to trios on average but 0.3 to the best trio. At real prevalence, the pipeline sent 94 of 96 included studies to human reading in the benchmark collections and 163 of 178 in the 2026 reviews (12.1% of 12,196 records sent to reading); its more sensitive voter alone sent 259 of 274 with 12.0%, at under a quarter of the machine cost. Conclusion: Because LLM errors are correlated, our results suggest two or three well-chosen models may suffice, but this needs deeper exploration in future studies. Which models are combined and how matter as much as how many, and any ensemble should be compared with its best single member.

title: HapAdapter: A Transfer Learning Protocol for DNA Foundation Models Adapted to Diploid Personal Epigenomes
desc: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the development of genomic language models (gLMs) that capitalize on the key features of natural language present in biological sequences. Moreover, DNA foundation models, a sub-class of gLMs, have demonstrated impressive accuracy in predicting a wide range of functional tracks from DNA sequence input. However, current DNA foundation models are exclusively trained on haploid reference genome sequences -- despite personal and graph genomes becoming the new standard for genomic analyses. This is principally because the cost to train gLMs on a personal diploid genome for a single individual is not currently practical. To help reconcile this disconnect between the current available use-cases of DNA foundation models with the modern direction of genomic sequence analysis, we present HapAdapter, a transfer-learning protocol that builds a small Siamese network on top of any pre-trained foundation model to enable inference from full diploid personal genome context. To demonstrate the utility of this method, we train a set of HapAdapter heads to predict allele-specific effects across assays on two representative foundation model backbones: DNABERT-2 and AlphaGenome. We demonstrate that our lightweight adapter more than doubles DNABERT-2's allele-specific discrimination and triples AlphaGenome's (130% and 210% gain in AUROC above chance, respectively, averaged over nine assays).

Automated Trimodal Deep Learning Fusion of MRI, CT, and Endoscopy for Preoperative Differentiation of Sinonasal Inverted Papilloma and Malignant Transformation.
desc: [Current oncology (Toronto, Ont.)] Purpose: To develop and validate an automated trimodal deep learning fusion framework integrating magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and nasal endoscopy for preoperative differentiation between sinonasal inverted papilloma (SIP) and SIP-transformed squamous cell carcinoma (SIP-SCC). Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 849 patients with pathological diagnoses of SIP (n = 614) or SIP-SCC (n = 235) between October 2014 and August 2025. Three unimodal ResNet-based deep learning models were trained and validated using data from 743 patients with only one or two modalities. The trained networks then generated MRI, CT, and endoscopy probability scores for each of 106 separate patients with complete trimodal data. These scores were combined using logistic regression, with fusion performance assessed by five-fold cross-validation in the 106-patient cohort. In the reader study, its performance was compared with six physicians (three junior, three senior). Results: The trimodal fusion model achieved an out-of-fold AUC of 0.910. Its AUC was higher than that of CT (0.634; unadjusted p < 0.001; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and endoscopy (0.813; unadjusted p = 0.023; Holm-adjusted p = 0.045), but the difference from MRI (0.859; unadjusted and adjusted p = 0.142) was not statistically significant. At the fixed threshold of 0.5, the fusion model achieved an accuracy of 83.0%. Accuracy differed significantly between the fusion model and the junior-reader group majority vote (64.2%; unadjusted p = 0.004; adjusted p = 0.022), but not the senior-reader group majority vote (81.1%; unadjusted p = 0.860; adjusted p = 1.000). Conclusions: By integrating MRI, CT, and endoscopy images, the trimodal fusion model achieved the highest AUC among the evaluated models for differentiating SIP from SIP-SCC, suggesting its potential value as a clinical decision support tool.

title: Capturing human expertise for AI-assisted molecular structure annotation
desc: We developed a large language model-based tool that captures expert reasoning in bile acid structure elucidation, drawing on hand written notebooks, scientific literature, and recorded voice-to-text analytical sessions. It generates human-readable reports detailing evidence for and against candidate structures, tracing each inference to its source and identifying ambiguities. When applied to data, the tool proposes bile acid conjugates lacking reference spectra.

title: Rethinking radiation dose optimization in pediatric computed tomography imaging: emerging algorithms and clinical integration.
desc: [Pediatric radiology] The optimization of radiation dose in pediatric computed tomography (CT) is a critical imperative, driven by the heightened radiosensitivity of children. This review provides a critical analysis of the evolution of dose optimization, from foundational principles like As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) and conventional techniques to the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI). We trace the progression from iterative reconstruction (IR), which offered initial dose reduction but was limited by unnatural image textures and computational demands, to the new paradigm of deep learning reconstruction (DLR) and emerging detector technologies like photon-counting CT. Clinical evidence demonstrates that DLR significantly shifts the traditional compromise between dose and image quality, enabling substantial potential dose reductions while producing images with superior noise properties and diagnostic confidence. Beyond reconstruction, AI is also automating scan protocoling to enhance consistency and reduce errors. However, the clinical integration of these powerful tools is not seamless. Significant barriers remain, including the "black box" nature of algorithms, the need for new training curricula for radiographers, and complex ethical and regulatory challenges. This review synthesizes these issues and charts a path forward, advocating for a holistic approach involving complementary AI-specific reference levels, federated learning, and robust governance to realize the full potential of a safer, more efficient, and patient-specific dose optimization ecosystem.

title: Adaptive Representations for Real-World Enzyme Optimization
desc: Protein fitness landscapes are highly rugged, giving rise to complex optimization landscapes. Bayesian optimization (BO) with Gaussian processes (GPs) is widely used in protein engineering for its sample efficiency and calibrated uncertainty estimates. Here, we study a joint fine-tuning framework of a protein language model (PLM) and a GP across enzyme fitness landscapes that span various distinct mutation regimes encountered in real-world engineering campaigns. Joint fine-tuning optimizes the PLM and GP parameters together in an uncertainty-calibrated manner, providing an adaptive representation that utilizes the information from previously acquired points in addition to the existing knowledge from pretraining. Across seven combinatorial enzyme landscapes, this approach yields a median relative improvement in top-5% coverage of 45% over one-hot encoding and 120% over mean-pooled static ESM-C embeddings. We further explore several new pooling strategies beyond standard mean pooling within the joint fine-tuning framework and show that mutation-site pooling, which localizes the representation to mutated residues, is the most consistent performer across all landscapes, outperforming both established baselines and alternative pooling schemes. Finally, we show that the finetuned approach makes more effective use of training-split information, yielding better coverage across test-split BO rounds. These results suggest that adapting the representation during a campaign, rather than fixing it in advance, is the better design choice for BO-guided enzyme engineering.

title: Artificial intelligence-assisted semi-automated personal health data curation and reuse for myocardial infarction.
source: PubMed · European heart journal. Digital health
desc: [European heart journal. Digital health] Digital applications have high potential in myocardial infarction management. This study aims to harmonize personal health data using a workflow driven by an Artificial Intelligence-assisted virtual assistant prototype, then reuse the data to facilitate the creation of standardized patient summaries and risk assessment. The required configurations for data documentation and curation were developed to drive the workflow execution. With consent and data transfer agreements, data of patients with myocardial infarction were extracted from multi-source medical records, structured, and ingested into the workflow. After transformation, personal health data were mapped into concrete clinical concepts connected with specific relationships defined by the reference ontology, forming source health knowledge graphs as the basic structure of personal health knowledge graphs. Then the constructed graphs were validated using Shapes Constraint Language-based constraints, triggering the human-in-the-loop process to enhance data quality. Information queries were conducted for data reuse. Thirty eight out of 45 planned patients were recruited with signed informed consent. Thirty patients finalized the study. The overall successful data ingestion rate is approximately 83%. The average data quality score is 95.45/100. Constructed personal health knowledge graphs can be reused to represent medical information as an international patient summary and evaluate individual risk of future cardiovascular events by calculating the Second Manifestations of Arterial Disease risk score. Our proposed workflow is feasible for semi-automated personal health data curation and secondary use. It provides a potential solution to enhance medical data interoperability, thereby facilitating risk assessment in cardiovascular diseases.

title: RBAi Scholar: Semantic and Hybrid biomedical literature Search for Researchers and AI assistants
desc: Motivation: A keyword search for mitochondrial dysfunction can miss a paper that says impaired mitochondrial function, so an empty result does not show that no such paper exists. Search by meaning addresses this mismatch, but it blurs exact strings such as gene symbols. Results: We present RBAi Scholar, which lets researchers and AI assistants search a growing corpus of biomedical abstracts by meaning (semantic search), by keyword, or by meaning among the papers that contain a required term (hybrid search). We tested it on a fixed version of 11.1 million records. For 500 questions worded unlike their target papers, semantic search placed the target in the top ten for 65.0%, against 18.6% for LitSense 2.0 and 0.8% for PubMed. OpenAlex semantic search, documented as using GTE-Large-EN embeddings, reached 27.8%. It reached 45.8% after OpenAlex rebuilt it with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, the model RBAi Scholar uses. Semantic search also led on the 380 held-out targets, which played no part in its design. Given one required term from the paper, hybrid search reached 93.9% on 328 held-out targets, against 42.1% for LitSense 2.0 with the same term. For 86 queries made of a paper's rarest identifier, such as a gene symbol, and two title words, keyword search reached 79.1%, against 34.9% for semantic search. When a blinded language-model judge graded the relevance of each system's top ten results, semantic search returned the most relevant results (nDCG@10 0.651 against 0.592 for OpenAlex semantic search with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B). Hybrid search ranked the target first more than twice as often as semantic search (50.0% against 23.3%). When we re-ran the searches for target papers on two cheaper index implementations and on the live service at 24.6 million records, every comparison kept its direction.

title: Evaluation of a Deep Learning Reconstruction Technique for Accelerated Brain MRI Scans.
desc: [Tomography (Ann Arbor, Mich.)] Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a cornerstone of diagnostic imaging, providing exceptional soft tissue contrast and enabling detailed characterization of neurological, vascular, and musculoskeletal diseases. Despite its clinical utility, prolonged acquisition times remain a primary limitation of MRI. Extended scan durations increase patient discomfort, particularly in vulnerable populations, which elevate the risk of motion artifacts that can degrade image quality and necessitate repeat imaging. Recent advances in machine learning, especially deep learning (DL), promise to ameliorate these limitations by enabling high-quality MRI reconstruction from heavily undersampled data, increasing throughput capacity and improving healthcare delivery efficiency. This work describes an FDA-cleared DL algorithm known as DeepFoqus-Accelerate for the reconstruction of deliberately under-sampled magnetic resonance imaging data. Fully sampled k-space from 408 brain MRI volumes (108 from 18 healthy volunteers and 300 from the public fastMRI dataset) was retrospectively undersampled. A detailed comparison of reconstructed images using DeepFoqus-Accelerate with corresponding fully sampled clinical images is presented using expert evaluation of overall image quality and quantitative similarity metrics. The only conventional comparator included in the study was GE's parallel imaging reconstruction (ARC) at matched retrospective undersampling; comparisons with compressed sensing and vendor-specific deep-learning reconstruction methods were outside the study design. This algorithm can allow for a four-fold reduction in brain imaging times relative to a fully sampled acquisition while preserving image quality. No reader rated any reconstruction below the acceptability threshold, and DeepFoqus-Accelerate exceeded ARC on all metrics at 4×. The findings characterize image quality and structural fidelity relative to fully sampled references and support further evaluation of diagnostic performance, with the potential to improve imaging efficiency and patient experience.

title: Resplitting LIT-PCBA with MolSCISSOR: A Memory-Efficient, Quasi-Deterministic Framework for Reducing Structural and Physicochemical Biases
desc: Reliable training-test partitioning is essential for developing and evaluating virtual screening (VS) methods, particularly in the era of machine learning (ML). However, existing molecular dataset splitting approaches do not simultaneously address key challenges in rigorous VS evaluation: cross-partition structural bias, test-set inter-class physicochemical bias, high memory requirements, limited scalability, stochastic allocation, a lack of automated optimization and of flexible training-test similarity control. We introduce MolSCISSOR, a lightweight, memory-efficient, quasi-deterministic framework for stratified data partitioning that integrates clustering and training-test allocation through multi-objective optimization. MolSCISSOR is used to repartition LIT-PCBA, a well-established VS benchmark comprising 15 target-specific datasets of experimentally confirmed actives and inactives, exhibiting substantial class imbalance, many of which are large-scale. We show that simple baseline ML models achieve significantly above-chance screening performance on the original AVE-derived partitions, indicating residual biases. The MolSCISSOR-generated benchmark, SPLIT-PCBA, is more challenging than both the AVE variant and that obtained using a BitBIRCH-Lean clustering-based workflow, with stricter cross-partition structural separation and improved physicochemical balance between test-set actives and inactives. MolSCISSOR mitigates stochastic variability, requires less memory than AVE, Lo-Hi and DataSAIL, and supports multiple split configurations with varying cross-partition similarity. MolSCISSOR and SPLIT-PCBA are freely available at https://github.com/caominhtr/molscissor and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23942580.

title: AI-integrated versus Standard Mammography Screening Pathways: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Accuracy.
desc: [Radiology. Imaging cancer] Purpose To compare the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated and standard mammography screening pathways for breast cancer detection using Bayesian network meta-analysis. Materials and Methods This prospectively registered review searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science through March 20, 2026, for diagnostic accuracy studies comparing two or more human-only or AI-integrated screening pathways using digital mammography or tomosynthesis. Bayesian bivariate random-effects network meta-analyses were fitted to a primary four-node and a secondary six-node network; risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 3 (QUADAS-3) and QUADAS-C tools, and certainty was graded using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Results Thirty-eight studies, with more than 4.2 million examinations, were included. In the primary digital mammography network (15 studies), AI as an independent reader (sensitivity, 78.9%; specificity, 95.8%) performed similarly to double human reading (sensitivity, 77.7%; specificity, 96.2%). In the secondary network, AI reader assistance had the highest sensitivity (86.8%) and AI triage had the highest specificity (96.4%). Per 10 000 screened (prevalence, 0.8%), AI reader assistance detected nine more cancers than single human reading (69 vs 60), with 77 additional false-positive recalls (558 vs 481); AI triage had 27% fewer false-positive recalls than single human reading (353 vs 481), with the same cancer detection as double human reading (64 vs 64). Stand-alone AI had the lowest specificity (93.0%) and the most false-positive recalls (n = 694). Rankings are hypothesis-generating: Top-ranked pathways had overlapping credible intervals. Conclusion In this synthesis, AI reader assistance was associated with the highest cancer detection and AI triage with the lowest false-positive recall; stand-alone AI was not supported as a primary screening strategy in settings with existing radiologist capacity. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Breast Cancer Screening, Diagnostic Test Accuracy, Deep Learning, Digital Mammography, Mammography, Network Meta-Analysis, Screening Pathway, Computer-aided Diagnosis Systematic review registration no. INPLASY202630080 Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Hidden Pitfalls of artificial intelligence in pediatric emergency radiology: a pictorial review of failure modes, clinical implications, and mitigation strategies.
desc: [Emergency radiology] Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming diagnostic radiology, yet its current clinical application in pediatric imaging remains fraught with challenges. Considerations that are unique to pediatric patients, including vast variations in developmental anatomy, age-specific disease patterns and pathologies, and technical variability create diagnostic challenges for which many commercially available AI systems, trained predominantly on adult data, are ill-equipped. This review utilizes literature evidence and illustrative clinical cases to critically examine various weaknesses of AI in pediatric imaging. Common pitfalls include misclassification of normal developmental variants, inability to distinguish pathological mimics, vulnerability to motion artifacts, modality-specific limitations, and errors introduced by artifacts or confounders. These failures are amplified by limited pediatric training data, annotation bias, and lack of contextual integration. We propose a structured framework for mitigating these risks, including pediatric-specific data curation, contextual model adaptation, algorithmic transparency, integrated feedback systems, technologist training, case-appropriate sedation planning, and centralized error tracking. These interventions are essential to enable safe, reliable, and ethically responsible AI deployment in pediatric emergency radiology.

title: AI-Assisted Lipid Nanoparticle Design for In Vivo mRNA Delivery: A Multiscale Therapeutic-System Engineering Framework.
desc: [Pharmaceutics] Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have rendered mRNA therapeutics clinically viable, yet their design remains impeded by tightly intertwined chemical, physical, biological, and manufacturing variables. This review argues that artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted LNP design should be approached as multiscale therapeutic-system engineering rather than reduced to isolated predictive tasks. We propose that AI models must holistically integrate ionizable lipid chemistry, supramolecular assembly, protein corona remodeling, endosomal escape, organ- and cell-specific tropism, cargo attributes, safety profiles, and process robustness into a cohesive framework. Current studies demonstrate that machine learning can prioritize ionizable lipids, predict formulation properties, guide tissue-selective delivery, and expedite the design-build-test-learn cycle. However, many models remain constrained by insufficient sample sizes, poor in vitro/in vivo translation, reliance on random-split validation, and narrow potency-centric endpoints. We propose and apply a claim-specific evidence hierarchy for AI-LNP studies and propose standardized multimodal datasets, mechanism-informed descriptors, scaffold-level holdout tests, and manufacturability-aware objective functions. We conclude that digital models of LNP delivery must be treated as emerging hypotheses until anchored by prospective and clinically relevant evidence.

title: Digital transformation of neonatal neurocritical care: Integrating telemedicine, multimodal monitoring, and precision neuroprotection.
source: PubMed · Seminars in fetal & neonatal medicine
desc: [Seminars in fetal & neonatal medicine] Neonatal brain injury remains a major contributor to mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability worldwide. Over the past two decades, neonatal neurocritical care (NNCC) has emerged as an interdisciplinary model focused on early diagnosis, continuous neuromonitoring, and neuroprotective interventions. Digital health technologies are now accelerating this transformation by expanding access to specialized expertise, enabling remote neuromonitoring, and supporting more standardized and individualized care across geographically distributed neonatal intensive care units (NICUs). This review discusses the evolving roles of telemedicine, multimodal monitoring, immersive technologies, artificial intelligence, and digital data ecosystems in NNCC. We explore current clinical applications, implementation challenges, and future perspectives, including precision neuroprotection, predictive analysis, and longitudinal digital neuro-NICU models. By integrating these technologies, digitally connected NNCC may help shift the field from reactive treatment of established injury toward proactive, precision-based neuroprotection focused on lifelong brain health.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Motivation, and Burnout Among Radiologists and Radiation Oncologists.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology
desc: [Journal of medical imaging and radiation oncology] Burnout is a major concern across medical professions, with radiologists and radiation oncologists among the most affected. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to reduce burnout by decreasing workload; however, previous research has shown inconsistent associations between AI use and burnout. These relationships may depend on clinicians' motivation for using AI. A 6.5 min anonymous online survey was distributed to members of the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists (RANZCR) over a 2 month period (May-July 2025). Measures included demographics and work-related variables (hours, level of training), burnout, AI use (frequency and task type), and motivation to use AI (based on Self-Determination Theory). Motivation was examined as a moderator of the relationship between AI use and burnout. Responses were received from 121 clinicians (90 radiologists, 31 radiation oncologists), including 21 trainees. Clinically significant burnout was reported by 42.1% (51/121) of respondents. Ninety-one (75.2%) respondents reported using AI, primarily for image analysis and interpretation (radiologists) and treatment planning (radiation oncologists). There was no overall significant relationship between AI use and burnout. However, AI use was positively associated with burnout among those reporting lower autonomy in AI use. This relationship was not mediated by need satisfaction or frustration. AI use is common among RANZCR members, and the burnout rate is prevalent. These preliminary findings highlight the potential importance of supporting autonomous motivation when implementing AI, while recognising that larger and more context-specific studies are required to confirm this relationship.

title: Cardiovascular Assessment of the Athlete's Heart: From Electrocardiography and Multimodality Imaging to Genetic Testing and Shared Decision-Making.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Sustained athletic training induces structural, functional, and electrical cardiac remodeling, collectively termed the "athlete's heart," which may phenotypically overlap with inherited and acquired cardiomyopathies. Distinguishing benign exercise-induced remodeling from occult heart disease is critical, since diagnostic error in either direction carries meaningful consequences, ranging from unwarranted sports disqualification to failure to identify athletes at risk of exercise-related sudden cardiac death. In this narrative review, based on a PubMed/MEDLINE search of the literature published between 2015 and 2026, we summarize the contemporary cardiovascular assessment of athletes, including electrocardiography, echocardiography with speckle-tracking and myocardial work, exercise testing, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), cardiac computed tomography, nuclear imaging, genetic testing, detraining, sex-specific considerations, and artificial intelligence (AI). Electrocardiography interpreted according to the International Criteria, echocardiography and, when indicated, CMR form the core of the evaluation, whereas the other tools are complementary and reserved for selected clinical questions. Many proposed numerical cut-offs derive from single cohorts and are not interchangeable across vendors, protocols, sexes, ethnicities, and sporting disciplines, and some athletes remain indeterminate despite comprehensive evaluation. We propose a pragmatic, non-validated stepwise framework that keeps diagnostic classification, arrhythmic risk assessment, and sports eligibility distinct and emphasizes multidisciplinary shared decision-making.

title: Evaluating a ChatGPT Standardized Patient for Adolescent Contraceptive Counseling: Mixed Methods Pilot Study.
desc: [JMIR medical education] This mixed methods pilot study, to develop and preliminarily evaluate a customized ChatGPT-based adolescent standardized patient to support clinicians in practicing person-centered contraceptive counseling, found that participants rated the AI simulation as highly feasible, acceptable, and appropriate, though automated grading showed limited agreement with human raters and requires further validation, supporting the simulation's perceived utility rather than reliable automated assessment.

title: Diabetic retinopathy feature utilisation in 54 convolutional neural networks: A heatmap analysis.
desc: [Acta ophthalmologica] To investigate how artificial intelligence (AI) systems detect referable diabetic retinopathy (DR) from retinal photographs by analysing heatmap patterns and determining their overlap with DR features. Fifty-four AI systems were developed using 27 backbone architectures, with each implemented as both binary-referable and multi-class grading models based on the International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) grading scale. Models were trained on DDR, BRSET and Kaggle datasets. After training, each model analysed 749 images with DR feature annotations, with Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, LIME and SHAP heatmaps generated and compared to pixel-level annotations of microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities and neovascularisation. All models achieved acceptable predictive performance (AUROC >0.8 for most architectures). Heatmap analysis revealed consistent attention to the central and temporal macular region. Exudates and cotton wool spots were highlighted most frequently by the heatmaps, with venous beading and neovascularisation at the disc showing poor overall coverage for binary referable classifiers. Models grading per the ICDR scale demonstrated higher coverage for all features. Substantial variability was observed between architectures, suggesting different feature detection capabilities. Interestingly, the heatmap analysis indicated that the models may be using different features to the ICDR grading scale definitions. AI models do not uniformly correlate with all DR features when detecting referable DR, limiting their predictive performance in unusual presentations. Heatmap aggregation analysis provides a scalable method for analysing model behaviour, allowing strengths and weaknesses to be assessed. These findings may help improve clinicians' trust and acceptance of AI.
